metaDesc: A cross-province 3-day, 2-night route through Kamphaeng Phet and Tak, Thailand: the World Heritage ruins, the Doi Musoe drive, Tak old town, Bhumibol Dam and the Mae Sot border, with real timings, prices and local food stops.

h1:
Kamphaeng Phet & Tak
3 Days, 2 Nights in the Lower North
intro: Kamphaeng Phet and Tak are neighbouring provinces less than an hour apart by car, yet they feel like two different worlds. One is a quiet World Heritage city of red brick and big shade trees; the other is a river town on the Ping that climbs into the mountains, drops down to a giant dam, then runs all the way to the Myanmar border at Mae Sot. We've mapped a 3-day, 2-night route that pulls both provinces into a single trip, with timings, prices and real places to eat along the way.

blocks.html: The Kamphaeng Phet–Tak route works best if you have your own car or a rental, because the sights are spread out and public transport between them is awkward. The town centres of Kamphaeng Phet and Tak sit about 65–70 km apart on Highway 1 (Phahonyothin), roughly an hour's drive. From Tak town over to Mae Sot you cross the Thanon Thang Sai range on Highway 105, a winding mountain road that takes about another hour and a half. This plan moves steadily from east to west so you never have to double back.

items: Day 1 — World Heritage Kamphaeng Phet: the historical park and the forest-temple (Aranyik) zone, overnight in Kamphaeng Phet town.
Day 2 — Drive into Tak town, up to Doi Musoe and its hill-tribe market, then the Trok Ban Chin old quarter, overnight in Tak or push on to Mae Sot.
Day 3 — Mae Sot: Wat Thai Wattanaram and the Rim Moei border market (or swap in Bhumibol Dam if you'd rather a water-and-nature day).

blocks.title: Pick your theme before you set off
blocks.html: Tak splits into two routes. There's the mountain-and-border line (Doi Musoe + Mae Sot + Rim Moei) and the water line (Bhumibol Dam, boat trips on the reservoir). They sit in opposite directions, so it's hard to do both in a short trip. With only 3 days, pick one line and you won't wear yourself out.

blocks.html: Start at Kamphaeng Phet Historical Park, a World Heritage Site that plenty of people drive straight past without realising what's there. The red brick and laterite among the big old trees give it a different feel from Sukhothai and Ayutthaya — quieter, with far fewer visitors.

items.activity: Kamphaeng Phet Historical Park, the walled-city zone
items.note: Open 08:30–16:30 daily, 10 THB for Thai visitors. Start at Wat Phra Kaeo in the centre of the old city.

items.activity: The Aranyik zone — Wat Phra Si Iriyabot, Wat Chang Rop
items.note: Just north of the city wall, about a 5–10 minute drive on. Wat Chang Rop has a beautiful base of elephants ringing the chedi.

items.activity: Lunch in town: noodles or rice-and-curry
items.note: The town centre has plenty of made-to-order spots and noodle shops, especially along Thesa Road.
See the bronze Shiva and other artefacts dug up around the old city — good background before you walk the temples.

items.activity: Stroll along the Ping River, municipal park
items.note: Cooler breeze in the late afternoon — nice for photos and a snack.

items.activity: Dinner + overnight in Kamphaeng Phet town
items.note: Town hotels start around 600–1,200 THB a night. Pick one near the night market to make finding food easy.

blocks.title: Take home some Kamphaeng Phet kluai khai
blocks.html: Before you leave town, grab some kluai khai — the small egg bananas the province is known for. You'll find them fresh, candied and as dried banana paste at the roadside souvenir stalls along the Asia Highway.

blocks.text: Day 2 — Up to Doi Musoe and Tak old town

blocks.html: Leave Kamphaeng Phet early and drive north on Highway 1 for about an hour to reach Tak town, then turn onto Highway 105, the Tak–Mae Sot road, to head up the mountain. This stretch is winding and steep, so drive carefully — but the views on both sides are worth it.

items.activity: Leave Kamphaeng Phet, drive to Tak town
items.note: About 65 km, roughly an hour.
A market run by the Musoe (Lahu) hill tribe selling vegetables, cool-climate fruit, avocados, oranges and mountain coffee. There's an old market and a new market about 1 km apart.
Noticeably cooler up here than down below — a good spot to rest before the drive back down.

items.activity: Back down into Tak town for Tak-style noodles
items.note: Tak's signature noodles come in a clear pork-bone broth with minced pork. Pa Mali is a long-running shop that locals often point you to.

items.activity: Trok Ban Chin, the old quarter on the Ping River
items.note: An old wooden-house neighbourhood of the historic Chinese community, with small cafés and shops and a retro feel — easy walking and photos.

items.activity: Walk the Rattanakosin Bicentennial bridge for sunset over the Ping
items.note: An old wooden suspension bridge in the middle of town, with a lovely river view in the evening.
If you're heading to Mae Sot the next day you can stay in Tak and leave early, or drive up and sleep in Mae Sot instead (about another 1.5 hours).

blocks.text: Day 3 — The Mae Sot border, or Bhumibol Dam

blocks.html: The last day gives you two choices. If you want a taste of the Myanmar border, head to Mae Sot. If you'd rather have a nature-and-water day, swing by Bhumibol Dam on the way home. We'd point culture-and-market people towards the Mae Sot route.

blocks.label: Day 3
blocks.title: Mae Sot, Rim Moei and the Myanmar border

items.activity: Drive from Tak up to Mae Sot on Highway 105
items.note: About 80 km via Doi Musoe, roughly 1.5 hours. If you stayed in Mae Sot, you can start right here.
A golden Burmese-style temple with a replica of the Mahamuni Buddha from Mandalay, in Tha Sai Luat sub-district near the border.

items.activity: Rim Moei market on the Moei River
items.note: A border market opposite Myawaddy in Myanmar, selling Burmese local goods, jewellery, jade and unusual snacks.

items.activity: Lunch: Burmese and Shan food in Mae Sot
items.note: Mae Sot has plenty of Burmese and Shan restaurants — try khao man som tam, khanom jeen nam ngiao or a Burmese tea.

items.activity: Walk Mae Sot municipal market for souvenirs
items.note: Popular buys are nuts, dried goods and woven textiles — stock up before you pack the car for the drive home.
Mae Sot back to Kamphaeng Phet is about 145 km, roughly 2.5–3 hours including the descent off the mountain.

blocks.title: The water alternative — Bhumibol Dam
blocks.html: If you swap Day 3 for Bhumibol Dam, drive from Tak town to Sam Ngao district, about 60 km. Bhumibol Dam is the largest curved concrete dam in Thailand, with a viewpoint along the crest and boat trips out on the reservoir. It suits anyone who'd take a lake setting over a border market.

blocks.text: Where to stay along the route

items.name: Stay in Kamphaeng Phet town (Night 1)
items.blurb: Pick a hotel near the town centre and the historical park, from around 600–1,200 THB, so you can walk the temples first thing in the morning.

items.name: Stay in Tak town (Night 2)
items.blurb: Hotels along the Ping River and in town, with easy onward travel to Mae Sot or Bhumibol Dam the next morning.

items.name: Stay in Mae Sot (optional)
items.blurb: If you drive up to Mae Sot on Night 2, you'll have an unhurried morning to see the temple and the Rim Moei market the next day.

items: Fuel + tolls — about 400–500 km in total, roughly 1,500–2,000 THB.
2 nights' accommodation — around 1,400–2,800 THB, depending on the hotel.
Entry fees — historical park and museum, a few hundred THB per person in total.
Food for 3 days — around 1,500–2,500 THB if you mostly eat at local spots.
Rough total — this trip for 2 people comes to around 6,000–9,000 THB.

faq.q: How far apart are Kamphaeng Phet and Tak — is it a long drive?
faq.a: Kamphaeng Phet town to Tak town is about 65–70 km on Highway 1, roughly an hour. From Tak town up to Mae Sot you cross the mountains for another 80 km or so, about an hour and a half because the road is so winding.

faq.q: Do I need my own car for the Kamphaeng Phet–Tak trip?
faq.a: We'd recommend your own car or a rental, because the sights are spread out and public transport between them is awkward — especially the climb up to Doi Musoe, the run to Mae Sot, and Bhumibol Dam, all of which sit outside the towns.

faq.q: Should I go to Mae Sot or Bhumibol Dam on the last day?
faq.a: It depends on your style. If you like culture, border markets and Burmese-style temples, go to Mae Sot. If you prefer nature, water and a lake setting, go to Bhumibol Dam. They're in opposite directions, so on a short trip you can only pick one.

faq.q: How long does it take to see Kamphaeng Phet Historical Park?
faq.a: Half a day is about right. Start in the walled-city zone at Wat Phra Kaeo, then continue to the Aranyik zone for Wat Phra Si Iriyabot and Wat Chang Rop. The park is open 08:30–16:30 daily; go in the morning or late afternoon, as the midday sun is fierce.

faq.q: When is the best time to do this route?
faq.a: Late rainy season into the cool season, roughly November to February, is ideal: the air on Doi Musoe is pleasantly cool, Bhumibol Dam's reservoir is full, and walking the historical park isn't too hot.
